utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've only asked the witness to remain outside because there is, I think, technically outstanding the issue of the 92 bis application in respect of which the Chamber sought a further filing from Mr. Kay. That's been provided. We haven't been in a position to provide further written material in the time available. We have, however, made available to you a draft of the proof of evidence of the witness concerned, which reveals how, of course, his evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll be handed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that it hadn't found its way to Your Honours yesterday. It was provided yesterday. It may be that the better course would be to put this consideration back rather than delay evidence. But our point arising from the draft proof of evidence is that, of course, all the matters that relate to the accused are going to be dealt with by the witness using the documents that we would prefer to be produced to you by 92 bis so that you can pre-read about the structure of the organisations concerned, and I simply repeat our argument last week that if at the end of the exercise it's found that anything admitted by 92 bis could or should be the subject of further evidence, it will be possible to identify it at that stage. And I have to say that the written filing of the amici doesn't, in our respectful submission, take the argument any further and doesn't identify any reason why this material shouldn't be before you in written form ahead of the witness coming to give evidence and it will save a great deal of time if you do have the material. We have to bear in mind that technically, and indeed in practice, Judges of this Chamber can't pre-read material in the form of witness statements although they are in a position to pre-read the summaries when they are provided in advance. And therefore, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I make two points?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of limited time in the last session, I had a very foolish question, but my concern was this: You didn't apply for the 92 bis, even if in bis form in case of C-037 or C-060, so what is the criterion? The only concern is time again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the concerns is time. That, of course, is a concern that we share with the Chamber and probably everybody else in the institution. What we've been doing with the first series of witnesses in this particular part of the case is tending to favour live evidence until the overall structure of the case is before you from at least one witness, and therefore we haven't in all cases been seeking out every little bit of evidence that might go in by 92 bis. I think I actually forecast that we might take this general approach at an earlier stage. If I didn't, then I should have done. We are now looking at all the forthcoming witnesses and looking in detail at what part or parts of their evidence might be properly advanced by 92 bis, and you'll be having a rolling series of motions dealing with all forthcoming witnesses in much the same way as you did in the Kosovo segment of the trial. And the priority given to time is much the same. It's just that the practicalities have changed. We feel we've passed the stage where it's desirable to take witnesses always in full and we've reached the stage where we must use 92 bis wherever we properly can. In this witness, the use of 92 bis would be rather different from in the case of many other witnesses because he's really providing a library of material to which he will himself turn wherever it's necessary. It's a question of getting that library of material before you in the most convenient way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then can I make another point? Being a little bit different from other Judges in the Tribunal, frankly, I'm not well familiar with the history of Croatia and Western Krajinas, so if I can hear the evidence live in the Court, I would find very useful, even if Prosecution could lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That will probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm speaking for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We quite understand that, and that evidence will in any event come in some form or another from the evidence of the witness that will be given live, because of course he'll be accounting for his own part in these events as well as pointing to the part in these events of the accused and he can only do that by giving a narrative history of the events in summary form in any event. As to Your Honour's earlier point, I'm asked by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff to draw to your attention that the amount of public documents available for this part of the case through this witness is radically different from the amount of public documents that there were available for C-037 or C-060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter now. I gather this witness isn't due until the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the earliest, no. Thursday, Friday. Can I, just while I'm on my feet, say I believe there are outstanding issues for resolution involving K38. It's our probably misunderstanding as to whether it's from us that you want the next initiative or whether we are awaiting a ruling from yourselves as to when that matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that matter is in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness is to be taken by Mr. Groome, and I'll hand the floor to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two applications prior to the witness being called. The first is, after discussing it with the witness, Prosecution is applying for a change in the protective measures. This witness has been given a new domicile in another country, a member state, has also been provided with identification papers of a different name. He no longer feels it's necessary to have his name disclosed [sic] from the public or his facial image distorted, and accordingly, the Prosecution at this time would move to withdraw or vary the Chamber's previous order for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll grant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the second matter, Your Honour, is that there are several pieces of evidence that the Prosecution would seek to tender through this witness that were not identified in the May submission of the 65 ter. Four of them are photographs that this witness provided to the Office of the Prosecutor which were in turn provided to Mr. Milosevic in May, attached to the statement, but they were not identified as potential exhibits. The second set of documents are -- involve the following: Two pieces of personal identification issued to this witness, which he produced; two lists of participants in international conferences of which this witness will testify he was one of those participants; a photograph of an arm patch; and an original military document given to this witness, which was then in turn provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm suggesting at this stage, Your Honour -- or I'm requesting at this stage if I may be permitted to show these exhibits to the witness and make an application for their admission into evidence at the time -- at the conclusion of the evidence in chief, when we will do this stock-taking procedure and examine the admissibility of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's any objection to admissibility, it can be made at the time the witness deals with the exhibit. Otherwise, for myself, I can see no reason why they shouldn't be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution calls Mr. Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Groome. Examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you moved to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1956.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that -- while in Sarajevo, did you attend university there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your field of study?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what languages you consider yourself able to speak fluently?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: English and French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to make pauses between question and answer for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention -- or can you describe for the Chamber an organisation known as KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a JNA military organisation with two streams; one deals with internal security and one with external security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you, if you can, to speak a little bit slower to assist the interpreters in translating.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you first become aware of this JNA military organisation known as KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In 1968, I was approached by one of the officers of the KOS to start working for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of the person who approached you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you meet Nikola Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Through my father, who used to be a member of then known UDBA, which grows into the state security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your initial meeting with Mr. Zimonja, did you have an ongoing relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us the nature of your relationship with Nikola Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mostly I had to deal with infiltration of different organisations. For example, in 1968, I was tasked with infiltrating the student movement in Sarajevo, and for example, planting the films on German tourists, for example, or infiltrating the Serbian emigres in UK, Croatia, Australia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider Nikola Zimonja to be your supervisor in KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of the time that you spent in Australia, working in the Croat emigre community in Sydney?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly, I have tried to penetrate the organisations. Unfortunately, I wasn't very successful. But I did spend 11 years in Australia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were asked to return to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, back in 1993, prior to the Winter Olympics in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who asked you to return to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you assigned to work in the -- work in connection with the Winter Olympics in Sarajevo in 1984?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been assigned to be a personal assistant to director of protocol of International Olympic Committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you held this post, did you still consider yourself to be a member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1984, were you given another assignment by Mr. Zimonja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been given assignment to go and join Agrokomerc in Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of that company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask now that a binder of exhibits containing 15 tabs - I apologise - 14 tabs be assigned a number, and I would then ask that the exhibit in the first tab be put on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 348.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if it's just my terminal, but when I -- I apologise. It's now up on the screen. I will be asking Mr. Lazarevic to describe a number of different people, most of which are contained in this summary diagram. I'm going to ask that it be left on the overhead projector during the course of his explanation, and at the conclusion of his description of these people, I will ask him to use this diagram to describe the relationships between the various people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I want to begin by asking you about two people associated with the Republic of Serb Krajina army, and during the course of your testimony, I will refer to them as the ARSK. The first person I want to ask you about is General Mrksic. Are you familiar with General Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Chamber who he is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic was a commanding officer of the 8th Operational Group in RSK when I joined them in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say the 8th Operational Group, do you mean of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I had an opportunity of meeting him again when he returned to Krajina in 1995 as a commanding officer of the RSK army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with him regarding Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please summarise that conversation for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: General Mrksic always believed that it was one of his very important military victories during the conflict, and he viewed it as a hospital being taken on the fourth floor by the Croatian forces and he had given -- ordered those forces to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you who he gave that order to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think the gentleman was a major at the time, Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you the words that he used when he gave Sljivancanin the order regarding Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the benefit of the Court, I will say that in English and Serbian. The Serbian expression, [Interpretation] "Kill those shits." [In English] My apologies to the Court. "Kill those shits."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with a person by the name of Lieutenant Colonel Mile Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe who he is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mile Novakovic is also a JNA officer who spent a considerable time in RSK, the various positions within the army structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he part of a Serbian military delegation at a number of international peace conferences?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about the 21st Corps. Can you tell us, was that a component of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The 21st Corps came into being after the JNA withdrew from Croatia. The 21st Corps actually held the responsibility in the area of Kordun, therefore the name Kordun Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the 39th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It's also known as the Banija Corps. That would be the eastern flank of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 15th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 15 Corps was also known as the Lika Corps, and that would be the western flank of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that the 21st Corps, the 39th Corps, and the 15th Corps are all corps within the ASRK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time period of the testimony you will give, did the 21st Corps have three different command centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On three occasions we have changed our HQ. Original was set in Topusko - that's in 1992 - on a little hill across from the compound of the UN sector compound. We have moved that HQ to Petrova Gora, used to be a JNA installation, and then from Petrova Gora to vicinity of Vojnic was the third and the last displacement of the HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us when the headquarters was moved to Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would be early 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us when it was moved to Vojnic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the same year, at a later stage, when the Serbian MUP moved into Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when you as a member of KOS, JNA military intelligence, were assigned to work as part of the 21st Corps in the ARSK army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when it was you were assigned to work there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your time with the ARSK, did you move to the different command centres as the headquarters moved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not. I kept my office in vicinity of the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In Topusko, to facilitate the meeting between myself and the liaison officer of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe who Colonel Bulat is for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Bulat is commanding officer, or used to be commanding officer, of 21st Corps, Kordun Corps, and also my CO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he somebody that you had daily contact with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Every single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of what contact, if any, he had with the General Staff of the Yugoslav army during the time he was head of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He had contact on a daily basis, every morning, after the briefing of his officers. He will also report directly to the General HQ in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any particular contacts that he had in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was present in the office when he made those calls on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the people or persons that he was speaking to in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that Momcilo Perisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your interaction with Colonel Bulat in the 21st Corps, can you describe for us what authority he had to make decisions in his area of responsibility, in the Kordun area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the benefit of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Anything that had to deal with things of local importance; movement of troops from one part of Kordun to another part of Kordun would be his individual decision, he would not have to report to Belgrade. Anything which would have wider implications to the things happening in ARSK, he would have to consult Belgrade HQ and wait for approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Chamber some examples, specific examples, of situations where Colonel Bulat would have to consult with General Perisic before taking action in Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: For example, if attack was being contemplated against the 5th Corps, which is generally known as the area of the Bihac pocket, and it had to be in cooperation with other corps on the ground, whether they are in ARSK or Republika Srpska, those are the situations where directive would be gotten from the General HQ in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you describe the 5th Corps, are you talking about the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your contacts and work in the 21st Corps, are you able to describe whether or not Colonel Bulat spoke with Belgrade first or with his nominal headquarters in Knin first?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would really depend on the situation. As I have said before, if the situation demanded cooperation of more than one corps, he would speak to Belgrade first and then to Knin second. Anything of a local character, he would report to Knin first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about a component of the 21st --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a component of the 21st Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting the French coming through on the English channel. Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a component of the 21st Corps. Are you familiar with a unit called the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what was the function of this unit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The function of this unit, which numbered around 40 to 45 young men generally with very extensive criminal record, was to conduct so-called "dirty jobs," "prijavi poslovi," within the AOR of the 21st Corps. And I might add that every corps had one of those units, for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the other corps, were these units also known as the anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They might have a different names, but the reasons for their establishment was always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have described the members of this unit as having criminal records. Were the members of this unit official soldiers within the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they have. They have been a part of the general army structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have used the term "dirty job." Can you please describe for the Chamber the meaning of that term.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, all the task which your well-educated and normal JNA officer would refuse to do would be assigned to those units known as anti-terrorist units. Basically they are used to scare the people, they are used to create disturbances, and they are not removed from killing either Croats, Muslims, or even Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Young man whose nickname was Paraga. His real name is Sinisa Martic, and I believe he is no longer among living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who Colonel Pero Ajdinovic is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Pero Ajdinovic was a member of KOS also, but the one that dealt with internal security, and he's the one that actually formed this group originally, prior to establishment of the 21st Corps in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who Colonel Mlado Karan is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Mlado Karan is also Serb KOS, internal security, who had inherited the position from Colonel Ajdinovic when he returned to Belgrade, and also to cover the command of the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to both of these men as being members of KOS, are you referring to a different KOS unit in ARSK or are you referring to the same KOS that you belonged to or belonged to in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I refer to the one and the same, but I like to make perfectly clear there are two strains within the corps, two lines, if you like; one that deals with internal security of the country and another one which deals with external security of the country, of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which branch of KOS did these two men belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Internal security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the death of a person by the name of Dmitar Obradovic. Are you familiar with the circumstances surrounding his death?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Mr. Obradovic was mayor of Vrginmost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe, before telling us the circumstances of his death, can you explain to the Chamber who he was and what was his role in the events of the Krajina in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I had the great pleasure of meeting Mr. Dmitar Obradovic on various occasions in his meetings with ECMM and I always found him to be extremely intelligent and in possession of a number of documents which would prove whatever he was saying at the meeting. And his idea was actually of co-habitat, meaning that the Serbs and Croats can live together in Croatia as long as the Serbs accept a Croatian government as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he opposed to the formation of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In a sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he in favour of peaceful reconciliation with Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mayor Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mayor Obradovic was ambushed and killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that occur within the confines or the area of responsibility of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, only about 200 yards away from the HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three bodies have carried the investigation. One was carried by the 21st Corps, one by the local police, and one by the UN international police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by virtue of your position in the 21st Corps, did you have contact or were you involved within the investigation into his death?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have been, but more as an observer and helping hand in the case there is some misunderstanding, language barrier or anything like that. But I was present during the initial investigation of the murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The investigation conducted by the 21st Corp, what conclusions did they draw regarding how Mayor Obradovic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The official statement was that the Croatian terrorists have penetrated our border along the Kupa River, came to the vicinity of Topusko and shot Mayor Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that's an official statement. Was there another finding of the people who investigated his death from the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was done by the anti-terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you heard members of the anti-terrorist group discussing the killing of Mayor Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, yes. They have said to me on a number of occasions that that was a very patriotic thing to do at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time that Mayor Obradovic was killed, can you tell us what was your title within the 21st Corps, and describe briefly your responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I had a rank of lieutenant colonel and I was a liaison officer between the 21st Corps and any international organisation on the ground; UN or International Red Cross or ECMM, or anybody else, for that matter. Even a journalist, if they would come, they would report to me first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in connection with this killing, were you charged with the duty of forwarding to the United Nations or informing the United Nations the official finding that Mayor Obradovic had been killed by Croatian terrorists?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Actually, I have been given a letter of protest to take to the HQ of the UN and hand it personally to the general -- General Musa Bamayi, and he was a sector commander of sector north, which covered precisely the same area as the 21st and the 35th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you handed over this letter of protest, did you know its contents to be false?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was well aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now direct your attention to the police in the Republic of Serb Krajina. Can you please describe for us what you know about the police structure of the Republic of Serb Krajina during the time you were there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in real terms of police force, it was established along the same lines as any other police force in any other country, meaning they had their many servants, they had their different departments, they had their state security within the police department, which were directly responsible to the state security of Serbia, they would have their police stations, they would have their -- which are based generally on the same area as the different sectors of the UN were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Each of these sectors, did they have deputies responsible for the sectors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would have a deputy who was responsible directly to the Ministry of Interior, who was Milan Martic at the time; also there would be a chief of police stations who would be responsible to the deputy, the deputy then in turn to Minister of Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the duties and responsibilities would be for each of these deputies for each area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not quite understanding the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many deputies were there for each area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I know of four: That would be sector north, sector south, sector west, and sector east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In each one of these individual sectors, how many deputies were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There would be one deputy who was responsible directly to the Minister of Internal Affairs, Mr. Martic, but there would be a number of police stations which would have their own chief of police within the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This deputy, or the deputy for each sector, was that person responsible for the activities of uniformed police officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also for the civilian-dressed officers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your time in the Krajina, did you form an impression regarding who was paying for the police in the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They have been paid from the same source as the army did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, on a number of occasions I was there when what we generally term a money man would arrive from Belgrade with amount of money for distribution where each of the commanders would get the names of the people he's supposed to pay, go to the paymaster, collect the amount of money for his unit, and then distribute this money to the members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would this same paymaster be responsible for dispersing money to both police units and ARSK units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an event during which the paymaster was robbed on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. On evening of August 6th, 1995, during withdrawal of the Serb forces from Krajina, the paymaster claimed that within the convoy he was robbed of all the pays for everybody within the army and police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after he claimed to have been robbed, were any police officers paid that pay period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody got paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who Milan Martic was, briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Milan Martic is a man who had a rather dramatic success in a very short period of time; from being a commander of a very small police station in the middle of nowhere, around Knin, that numbered approximately four men, to becoming president of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to being station commander -- or I'm sorry. In between his positions as station commander and president of the Republic of Serb Krajina, did he hold other high-profile positions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was Minister of Internal Affairs prior to becoming president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you to describe for the Chamber what relationship, if any, existed between the ARSK and the RSK police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to describe, if you can, what was the relationship between the army and the police in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, the army had the upper hand in everything that was happening. When I'm talking about the beginning, I'm talking about 1992. Later on, with the presence of the special forces from Serbia, that power has gone into the hands of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the implications of the Vance plan on the army in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for us what the Vance plan required regarding the military.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Vance plan required total demilitarisation and demobile of all units within the RSK. Us being co-signatories of the plan, what we did, we changed the uniform overnight from military olive-green into the police blue and within a very short period of time, I'd say within ten hours, we have repainted all the military vehicles into the blue colour, being representing the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Vance plan put any restriction on the size of the police forces in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of transformation, were you issued an identification card describing you as a member of the RSK police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have been issued a card, and also I have been asked to remove my uniform, military uniform, and start wearing civilian clothing during this time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time you were issued an identification card for the RSK police, were you still a member of the JNA KOS unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, basically nothing has changed. We just changed the colour of the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 348, tab 2. It's a photograph, and I'd ask that be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you recognise the photograph that's now on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the people that are in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please, going left to right --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask the usher maybe to remain with the witness for a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you, moving from left to right, can you please identify them to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The person I'm pointing right now, it's me. Next to me, standing, is General Satish Nambiar, who was UN force commander for all of the area of the UN. General -- actually, there is another colonel here, a Polish colonel, but his name really escapes me, I can't remember. And here in the corner, unfortunately it's not very bright lit on my monitor here, you can see General Novakovic. Interesting part which I'd like to draw attention to, this is the time when we have actually demob'd and changed the uniforms into police. There is only shoulder patch you can see here written "milicija" in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a pen and circle the shoulder patch that you've just described as containing the words "police."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've used the word "milicija." Can you please describe the translation of that word for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's "police."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The handwriting on this photograph, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now ask that Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 3, be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, do you recognise what is depicted in Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my police ID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that issued to you at a time when you were a member of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When it's convenient, that can be removed from the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lazarevic, I'd like -- or ask you to describe for the Chamber the command structure of these military people that are now appearing in police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not following you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these former military people, did they fall into the command structure of the police? In other words, did they then take their orders from the local station commanders or did they have some separate command structure to the police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were never really a part of the police force as such, because they retained their ranks in a commanding chain within the military. What they did, they simply changed the uniform overnight, but the chain of command remained the same, and that was the JNA chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you familiar with an incident around March of 1992 when a large number of these men were brought back to Belgrade for a particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, March 1992 begins the withdrawal of the JNA as such back to the -- back to Bosnia, and through Bosnia back to Serbia proper really. A number of officers was left behind, and they are the regular JNA officers. Also, the HQ in Belgrade would go through the files of every JNA officer and by the place of birth, if the place of birth was in Krajina, or RSK, they would be sent back to Krajina for the stint of duty the length of six months, and then they had option either to return to Belgrade or to continue their service in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to what you've just described, was there a specific event in which volunteers were asked to volunteer to go to Belgrade to work on a specific project?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was the police force, not the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe what the police -- first let's clarify. What police force are you going to speak about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Regular police from the RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was -- actually, there was an order issued from Belgrade, order/request, if you like, that each of the sectors would send approximately 100 uniformed police officers to Belgrade. For that purpose, Belgrade has sent brand-new uniforms which are the same as the proper Serbian police would wear. Totally new uniforms. And they were to be transferred on the buses to Belgrade and to deal with demonstrators on the street in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the demonstration, was that a demonstration against Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many altogether of these Republic of Serb Krajina police were outfitted with Republic of Serbia police uniforms and transported to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I know for the fact that the area of the 21st Corps, or area of Kordun, had supplied 100 men for this particular task, and to my general knowledge, each of the other sectors have given the same number. So I would put the number to four to five hundred in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you deal with the time that this happened, Mr. Groome, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us your best approximation or the actual date, if you know, when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the Court is aware of how many demonstrations were there on Belgrade streets in this particular period of time. This one that I'm talking about has taken place in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of how the men were selected, how these 500 men -- 400 to 500 men were selected to go to Belgrade? What was that process like?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The bigger, the better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when anything was said to the men to -- in the section process?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a kind of standing joke at the time, because they were selecting really huge blokes, like you know, anything over six-two, to assign them to Belgrade and deal with the demonstrators, and most of them actually were joking, like, they're going to go over there and beat the living daylights out of the anti-communist demonstrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Republic of Serb Krajina police, did they also have a state security division or a DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had the head of this DB in RSK, in my sector, anyway, was a gentleman by the name of Milos Pajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that he was in charge of it, was he the person who was named as the head of the RSK DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On paper, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience, did you come to believe that somebody else was in fact in charge of the RSK DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Toso Pajic, who was to become Minister of Interior of RSK in 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what, if any, relationship you had with Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I always found Mr. Pajic to be a very pleasant, well-educated, and a kind of diplomatic person. I had to deal with him on a daily basis during my stay in Krajina, simply because he was also named as a liaison officer to the UN but like my police counterpart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your daily contacts with Mr. Pajic, did he discuss what, if any, relationship he had with the DB of the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On numerous occasions he stated that he actually works for Jovica Stanisic, who was head of the state security in Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he describe for you how often he was in contact with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Virtually, on a daily basis. On a few occasions, I was in his office. He had a direct telephone line to Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname or other name that he used when he referred to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He considered him to be his "Daddy," and generally referred to him always as "Daddy."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your conversations with Toso Pajic, did he also use a term to refer to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what term was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: "Boss."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your relationship with Mr. Pajic, did he ever describe for you his relationship with the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What my understanding was, that Mr. Pajic was actually full time employed by the DB in Serbia, because simply when we had returned to Belgrade in August 1995, he just resumed his old office in Belgrade within the DB structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask now that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 4, and that it be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise, Mr. Lazarevic, what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The place is a hotel in Topusko, and the three persons sitting there are, I'll go from left to right: That would be Mr. Toso Pajic, when he was chief of police of Vojnic, so that would be very early 1992, I'd put it down around May to June of 1992. This Danish officer here, I remember he was Danish, but he was in charge of IPTF, but I don't remember the name. And there's me, liaison officer of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your handwriting on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. That can be removed from the ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Djuro Skaljac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with Mr. Djuro Skaljac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber who he is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Djuro Skaljac is another police officer who was the second in charge in Vojnic. He was assistant to Mr. Toso Pajic. At a later stage, Mr. Skaljac has become a liaison police officer with Mr. Abdic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about one political figure from the Republic of Serb Krajina, and that is Mr. Goran Hadzic. Can you tell us briefly who he was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic was elected president of the RSK. I have attended quite a few meetings within RSK and also outside the RSK, the international meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic ever describe for you the nature of his relationship with Mr. Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think if I describe to the Court a little incident that happened probably will give the best picture of what he really felt. During one of the meetings in Norway that we had with the Croatian side, with the participation of the UN, of course, we had a little recess, we were sitting in an office separate from the other delegations, and Mr. Hadzic was sitting at another table, playing solitaire. Somebody knocked on the door and two ambassadors walked in; it was American ambassador at the time to Croatia, Mr. Galbraith, and a Canadian ambassador whose name I cannot recall, and addressed him as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Ambassador Galbraith addressed Mr. Hadzic as "Mr. President," which I translated to him as "Mr. President." Without lifting his head from the cards, he turned around and told me, "Well, tell him I'm not a president, I'm just a dispatcher." And I believe at that particular point in time Mr. Hadzic actually realised that he's just dispatching messages from somebody else to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about institutions, federal institutions in the former Yugoslavia, and I want to ask you a little bit more about your organisation, KOS, in the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, you described yourself, Colonel Pero Ajdinovic, and Colonel Mlado Karan as all being members of KOS assigned to work in the RSK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your work with KOS, did you come to be familiar with a term known as "black funds"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Actually, the Serbian expression for it is "crni fondovi."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what this term "black funds" refers to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It simply meant that you had a large amount of money at your disposal for which you did not have to sign or explain how it has been spent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to learn where much of this funding came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very early in the 1960s and 1970s, those funds were provided by the company by the name of Genex, General Export/Import, which everybody knew that it was actually a DB front outside of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're describing now this company as having this association with the DB. Did, despite that fact, did this company also provide funds which were used by members of KOS in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At certain locations, yes, specifically if it required a larger amount of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber the basis of your knowledge regarding black funds and other -- these financial matters related to KOS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll take myself personally. I have never signed for any receipt of the money from 1968 until 1995, and yet I have been financed on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beginning of your testimony, you described a number of overseas assignments that you had. Did you have access to what you're terming black funds during those periods of time as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would supply a request for a certain amount of money and then I would pick up, without any questioning, the amount that I have requested, without signing for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going into any great detail, could you list for the Chamber some types of specific expenses which would be -- which black funds would be used for?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, usually to deal with the people from other countries. Whether it's bribery, whether it's buying off documents, whether it's buying off weapons; depending really on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe -- did you also have access to more legitimate sources of funding in the course of your work with KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Once I have arrived in the Kordun area, I have been placed on a payroll of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for monies that you received for legitimate activities, can you describe the process for requesting and receiving those monies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There would be an "X" amount of money with a receipt, which was a formal receipt, which I would have to sign that I have received the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you made a request for some black funds to, let's say hypothetically, buy some information, was it expected that you would then produce that information shortly afterward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to discuss with Mr. Zimonja a request that you had for a large amount of black funds?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the incidents that comes to mind was an offer to buy a very extensive number of weapons and listening devices from Ukranian battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you regarding his ability to provide you with those funds?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He said the amount within itself would not pose a problem for them; however, that the army is not interested and that I should refer it to the DB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the DB become involved in this proposed purchase of weapons from the Ukranian battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After being given permission by Colonel Zimonja to go and visit Mr. Toso Pajic and to pass the offer to him, the phone call was made to Mr. Stanisic in Belgrade, to which reply was that hold onto it for a couple of days and he'll get back to Toso Pajic, and that was the last I heard of it. Whether they bought it or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you regarding black funds is: When you were overseas, can you describe for us briefly how black funds would be sent to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was rather a simple system and very workable. Within every embassy, no matter where it is - the Yugoslav Embassy, that is - there was always a little Yugoslav club adjacent to the embassy which would have a security officer in there. You would go in there, introduce yourself, show the passport and then ask are there any messages for you. I remember, for example, the London one. There was a number of pigeon holes with the letters of the alphabet and, "L" for Lazarevic, if they had anything in there, they would give it to me. On the other hand, if I had to forward any information or a report, I would go there, place an envelope, seal it, and place it in this "L" hole, and somebody would obviously, you know, send it where it was supposed to go. My request for funds would go absolutely the same way. I would write down the request, explain why I need this amount of money, place in envelope, put in the pigeon hole and maybe two days later come back and collect the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'd like to move from this topic and now ask you to describe for us the relationship between the Yugoslav People's Army, the ARSK - the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina - and whatever you are able to describe for the Chamber regarding the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Personally, my experience has shown that we are not talking about three different armies, we are talking about one and only army, and that's the JNA. Whether the name was VRS - Vojska Republika Srpska - or RSK army - Vojska Republika Srpska Krajina - was totally irrelevant in real terms, because all the supplies and the finances would come from Yugoslavia, Serbia, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time at the 21st Corps, did you come to know how -- or come to see supply convoys coming from the Yugoslav Armija in Serbia to the area of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. As frequent as at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the route that was taken?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would start from Belgrade, for example, and go through Posavina corridor, which is also known as "Zila Kucavica" in Serbian language, because that was the only corridor that connected the RSK with Serbia proper. Commonly go through there and arrive to our territory, and as it went through, to each of the command it would arrive to -- for example, if the convoy arrives to the area of 39 Corps, it would release a number of trucks by request of the 39th Corps, the rest of the convoy would continue, come the 21st Corps, we would take a number of trucks which were assigned to us, the rest of the convoy would continue to Lika Corps. And along the way prior to coming to us, I assume they would also release some of the trucks along Bosnian route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the Bosnian route, can you be more specific about --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Meaning the supplies to the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the manifest which would -- well, I have to clarify something to the Court here. Along all these major arteries, there was always a number of checkpoints manned by the police and the military. One of those checkpoints was in the vicinity of my post, which was very close to the UN. The reason why I frequented that particular point was because I didn't want too much of a harassment to the UN, so I tried to prevent that. At one particular instance I was there when a convoy actually arrived, they had a manifesto with them which showed that the convoy started with 30 trucks but at the time when they arrived to this particular checkpoint, they had probably around 15 trucks within the convoy, which is natural to assume that the 15 had been left behind at different stages of the route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your answer to a question a few minutes ago, you used the word "Zila Kucavica." Can you please translate that for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's "jugular vein," really. If you cut that one off, the life is gone. Given kind of a poetic description of this corridor, which if you cut it off, the life would simply die in RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your observations of these convoys during your time with the 21st Corps, are you able to estimate for the Chamber what percentage of weapons used by the 21st Corps were supplied from the Yugoslav army at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To be very conservative, I would place that 80 per cent of the weaponry was supplied from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the 21st Corps, were you ever aware of joint operations between the ARSK and the VRS, the army of the Republic of Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can you describe some of those for the Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Usually during the attacks on the Bihac pocket against the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army. The area of Bihac pocket was surrounded by the five corps. Three of those corps were from RSK and two corps from Bosnia, meaning Republika Srpska; 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps from the VRS, 39th Corps, 21st Corps, and the 15th Corps from RSK army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your knowledge of standard operating procedure and your actual experience in the 21st Corps, can you describe for the Chamber at what level that type of coordination would have to be decided at.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It had to be decided at the level of the General HQ in Belgrade. That was not a simple action. It required a lot of coordination and preparation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present in 1995 at a parade in Slunj in which VRS military equipment was displayed in a parade of which one of the participants was the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended that particular ceremony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about that ceremony in greater detail later in your testimony. Could I ask you to describe what significant pieces of military equipment were present that you recognised as being from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A large number of the rocket systems that came, including the multi-rocket launchers, Luna rockets, were actually convoyed from Bosnia or Republika Srpska into RSK for this specific purpose. They were brought in in the morning and they left Krajina the same day, in the afternoon, after the parade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back and ask you one more question regarding the convoys. During your experience with these convoys, did it ever come to your knowledge whether the manifests that you've described for us falsely described the contents, the actual contents of the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, on a number of occasions when, for example, it would declare as being humanitarian convoy. It would contain purely military elements in it, like ammunition or additional automatic weapons and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time serving with the 21st Corps, were there other members of the Yugoslav army assigned to work there on a temporary basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Within the RSK?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from the JNA officers, not any particular units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the approximate number of JNA officers that were assigned to work in the ARSK on a temporary basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would put it down to a full hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that all of the officers in the army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina were actually active members of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long would be the average stay of one of these officers before returning to the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The minimum was a six-months tour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your time at the 21st Corps, did you come to know some of these officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to state that their places of residence were from throughout Yugoslavia, not simply the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Mostly would be actually stationed in Belgrade originally, but there were people from Krusevac, from Nis, Dragojevac; all the places down further south in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these officers receive any enticements or extra benefits by virtue of their service in the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apparently, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us how you know? If you know what enticements they received, how do you know it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's start with being highly paid compared to the officers of the RSK army, which were promoted by Knin, not to mention that all of these people, officers, decided to stay longer than six months would be virtually guaranteed to receive the key to an apartment upon their return to Belgrade, or to wherever they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 5. I'd ask that the Serbian original be placed on the overhead projector and be placed in such a way that Mr. Lazarevic can see the signature on the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'd ask you to take a look at that document and ask you: Do you recognise the signature of the person who signed that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do you recognise that signature to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major General Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with his signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have seen it frequently enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to caution about one thing. This document originates from 1994, and the Prosecutor has, all the time until now, been talking about 1995, as well as about events from 1992, and later he did not continue to deal with documents related to the Croatian indictment after 1991. We have been examining documents related to events after 1992, including this one, which is from 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber what this document is, and describe its import to us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with new recruits for the army from the RSK. A number of young people, by the time they reach 19, because in Yugoslavia we always had a compulsory national service, they would come of age when they're supposed to do their national service. Now, this particular document will give the number and the area from which these people are supposed to come from and go to. The suggestion by the General HQ of Belgrade was to keep them in the area simply for two reasons: One, we need the manpower in uniform, with weapons. We can train them on the ground in real combat situation and instead of having 18 months of national service, we would cut it down to nine months, because it will take like double time in value.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct in stating that that document memorialises the fact that a person would receive credit for their service in the ARSK throughout Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, not from this document, no. But this is a general consensus. It was always like that in wartime. Any time that you spend in war is counted as double time towards your pension, or in this instance, towards your national service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now ask you about the state security service in the Republic of Serbia. You've already mentioned Mr. Stanisic. I want to ask you: Were you aware -- become aware that Mr. Stanisic was present in the RSK at any time you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I had the opportunity to meet the gentleman on two or three rather informal occasions in Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that he was present in relation to a dispute between Mr. Babic and Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I believe that particular meeting with Mr. Stanisic came from Belgrade carrying specific message from Mr. Slobodan Milosevic to Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From a general discussion with the people attending this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the times that you met Mr. Stanisic informally in the Krajina and this meeting that you've just described for us, did you also become aware of other times that Mr. Stanisic was present in the Krajina from your conversations with other officers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Toso Pajic would be the one, for example, to tell me that "Daddy was here yesterday" or "Daddy is planning to come next week" or something like that. But since I was not a part of the police force, I never attended those meetings, but I'm pretty certain that Mr. Stanisic did come reasonably frequently to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best you're able, can you approximate for the Chamber the first time you became aware Mr. Stanisic was present in the Krajina? And tell us the period of time -- or in other words, the last time that you were aware he was present in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That would be very difficult for me to say. I know at the beginning those visits were more frequent, I think probably due to organisational problems than anything else. At a later stage, Mr. Stanisic had his deputies, or his right hands, or whatever you want to call them, who were actually present on a daily basis within the RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the beginning," can you give us what time period you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would place that early 1990 through 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there ever come a time when Mr. Toso Pajic showed you a document from Mr. Stanisic regarding cooperation with Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a time when, for unknown reason to me, Fikret Abdic and Belgrade have reconciled. And the letter which arrived from Belgrade, not only through Stanisic, through Toso Pajic also, through the military channels, was to establish a good neighbourly cooperation with Abdic's forces, which were actually boarding with the 21st Corps area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally opposed to this cooperation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Not only me, but a number of officers were opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear: Fikret Abdic is a Bosnian, a Bosnian Muslim, who at some point entered into an alliance with members of the Serb Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Frenki Stamatovic, do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have met the gentleman also on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Chamber who he is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamatovic was also, for some unknown reason to me -- it's also spelled sometimes Simatovic and Stamatovic. I know him as Stamatovic, some people know him as Simatovic, but it's one and the same person, in any case. He was actually in possession of our former HQ in Petrova Gora. That's when he formed his own HQ with the special forces of the police from Serbia.
