utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what knowledge you have about these special forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Special forces were deployed in our area prior to establishment of a new HQ on the Bosnian side, in the vicinity of Velika Kladusa, code-named Pauk, meaning "spider."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These special forces, did they wear a particular emblem to identify themselves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a very distinguished-looking emblem, different to the regular RSK. It's an upside down sword with a Serbian flag beneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next exhibit I'd ask that the witness be shown is a photograph of an insignia. I would ask that a new Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number be assigned and that we designate it tab 1, as I expect that there will be additional insignias introduced during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 349.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'd ask you to take at look at what is now on the overhead and has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 349, tab 1. Do you recognise what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a shoulder patch on uniform of the special forces of the police from Serbia deployed in RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would members of this special forces unit attached to Frenki Stamatovic uniformly wear this identifying patch?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person by the name of Colonel Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have had the displeasure of meeting this gentleman only once, but I have seen him frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us who he was and what unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He belonged to unit from MUP Serbia, Ministry of Interior Affairs of Serbia. His rank was colonel. A very short-tempered, very interesting person. I have met him on a number of occasions within the HQ of the 21st Corps in discussion with Colonel Bulat. Once when I had a meeting with him personally, it did not end very happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us the period of time when you would see him regularly in the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the times that you would see him, would he be wearing the patch that you've just pointed to as Prosecution 349, tab 1?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and would also carry a rank of colonel on his shirt pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about what, if any, knowledge you have regarding Mr. Arkan. Do you know who Arkan is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic. Yes, I'm familiar with the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe whether or not you actually met him, and describe for us the circumstances of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was early 1992, in Hotel Topusko. JNA officers had a meeting how to alleviate the problems of the war, which, by signing all these differences per agreement, came to resemble the normalcy, how to improve the living standard in the area. During this particular meeting in Hotel Topusko, Mr. Raznjatovic walked in with three or four of his bodyguards and created a very unhealthy atmosphere by attacking these officers, saying, "You should be going out and fighting instead of planting trees." And you can tell, by looking at the faces of the people, they were actually afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any connections that Arkan may have had with the state security service of the Republic of Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Raznjatovic had a number of arrest warrants throughout Europe that I was familiar with, and yet he was never arrested in Yugoslavia, on request by the Interpol. So he was well protected in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that might be a good place to break, if the Chamber is considering a break at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn there. Mr. Lazarevic, in this adjournment and any others there may be during your evidence, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. That does include the members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be back, please, at half past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we ended this morning's session with you describing what you knew about Arkan. Are you able to describe for us what, if any, relationship Arkan's group, Arkan's Tigers, had with the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Arkan's forces were deployed in the Pauk HQ and were then put with the MUP of Serbia and the members of the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a number of detailed questions about this Pauk unit later in your testimony, but could you, in a sentence or two, describe for the Chamber: What was Pauk?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Pauk was an HQ established on the Bosnian side which the 21st Corps totally disclaimed as being part of us, which would allow for the members of the 21st Corps actually to go and fight against Bosnian 5th Corps on the Bosnian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this Pauk unit, can you tell us what units were combined to make this Pauk headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The members of the 21st Corps, officers and fighters; the members of Abdic's own forces; the members of Arkan's Tigers; and the members of the special police from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your observations or your knowledge of what occurred in Pauk, did you see Arkan's Tigers and members of the 21st Corps cooperating?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to an incident in a bar. Were you present in a bar when an incident arose with some of Arkan's Tigers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about a UN bar which was specifically for the UN members. The duty officer of the UN HQ came to my hut, it was late at night, like 1.00 or 2.00 in the morning, and told me that they have a problem with some Serbian soldiers. Me thinking probably, you know, when he says Serbian, meaning the RSK, I put a uniform on and brought in a jeep, went into the bar to find four members of Arkan's forces in there having drinks and taking cartons of cigarettes and refusing to pay for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that they were members of Arkan's group?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By their uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after arriving at this UN bar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the only possible thing I could do - because I couldn't deal with them - so I went back to the nearest phone and called my own HQ and asked for Colonel Bulat to be brought to the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to calling Colonel Bulat, did you attempt to resolve the situation by speaking to these members of Arkan's Tigers directly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They're the kind of people you don't talk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to contact Colonel Bulat?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Within about ten minutes they woke him up, he spoke to me briefly. I told him what problem I had, or rather, what the UN had, and he said to remain in vicinity and somebody will come there and fix it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just remind you, if you could slow down the pace, as an aid to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After speaking to Colonel Bulat regarding this problem, what, if anything, happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 30 minutes after I have concluded my conversation with Colonel Bulat, a jeep arrived, and in the jeep was a Colonel Pejovic, who was Arkan's colonel, with probably three or four members of his, I assume, MPs. I briefly explained what happened, he walked into the bar. I was following behind. He walked up to these four soldiers that were creating this disturbance. They stood at attention, he slapped each one of them so hard he actually brought them down to their knees. And the other MP just picked him up and took him out of the bar. I have never seen him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based upon your observations regarding this incident, did you conclude that Colonel Bulat had been in contact with Colonel Pejovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I came to understand he was in contact with Pauk HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you mean to ask whether he was in contact before he came to the bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Perhaps I'll try to clear it up with this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I was asking you, Mr. Lazarevic, was: Do you know how Colonel Bulat was able to have Colonel Pejovic and some other members of Arkan's men come to the bar to deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was a direct telephone line in Colonel Bulat's office with Pauk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pauk was the joint command that you described for us that included Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time that you were present with the RSK Minister of Defence, Mr. Dusan Rakic, when you came to have a meeting, or Rakic had a meeting with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a personal escort to Minister of Defence at the time, Admiral Rakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe where this meeting was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It took place in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I still believe that it was a chance meeting, because we were driving through -- we had a meeting in the sector east with the sector commander there, but as we were driving through Dalj, passing the petrol station, and there was a diner within the petrol station, I believe belonged to Mr. Raznjatovic, minister asked to stop the car because he saw Arkan there and the gentleman by the nickname of Badza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did your job as personal escort entail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was to translate for the Minister of Defence in his meeting with UN sector commander of sector east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this meeting, you've mentioned a person by the name of Badza, Arkan, and Minister Rakic. Was there anybody else present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A number of Arkan's men were in the restaurant, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person you've referred to as Badza, do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's -- he was a high-ranking police official from Serbia, and his name was Stojkovic or Stojilkovic or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before I continue with your testimony, I'm going to ask that you return to the exhibit that is on the overhead, Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 1. And if I could -- while we view on our monitors, I'm going to ask you to take the pointer. I'm going to ask you to describe now the relationships between the different people that you've testified about. And before I do that, I want to ask you about this exhibit. Is this exhibit based upon a sketch that you drew describing the relationships between the people named in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to begin with the green box on the right marked "JNA/VJ." Could you please describe for us the different relationships between the people.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The green box has a heading of JNA or VJ because the Yugoslav army changed its name to Vojska Jugoslavije later on. At the General HQ Main Staff, you have General Momcilo Perisic. And then you have your KOS command, you have two strains; one to the left is internal security, or the sector north RSK, Colonel Petar Surla and Colonel Mlado Karan. On the right-hand side, you have external security of the KOS, Colonel Nikola Zimonja. Following down, you go to General HQ in Knin, with General Celeketic and General Mile Mrksic connecting straight to the 21st Corps at which head is the commanding officer Colonel Cedo Bulat, and then you have me, C-001 here, being a liaison officer to Colonel Bulat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say connecting to Colonel Bulat. What does the line connecting to Colonel Bulat indicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There's a line that goes on both ends. If you follow to the left, you go straight to General HQ, and to the right goes to the internal security. And from internal security to actual General HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is clear, C-001, was that the code-name that you believed you would be testifying under here today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any reference to C-001 is really a reference to yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, underneath your C-001, there are three names that are bracketed and that there's a line connecting them. Can you please describe what that line represents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's the infamous anti-terrorist unit at which head was Colonel Pero Ajdinovic. Below that, you have the name of Sinisa Martic, with the nickname Paraga, and one of the fighters, Jovo Vojinovic, who became my personal friend during this time. And you can see the line going straight up to the internal security of KOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does the fact that the box for the 21st Corps, that fits wholly within the box for the JNA/VJ. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It indicates it's one and the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you now move to the blue box to your left, marked "SDB Serbia." Can you please describe the relationships depicted in that part of the diagram.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the head of the SDB Serbia at the time was Mr. Stanisic, Jovica. His direct assistants were Frenki, also known as Simatovic or Stamatovic, followed by Colonel Ulemek, or Legija, and Colonel Bozovic. And then within the circle you also see Mr. Toso Pajic was the chief of police and liaison officer of the RSK, and his direct line goes to the SDB Serbia Mr. Stanisic, and RSK MUP, Minister of Internal Affairs, also Milos Pajic, head of state security. And all connected directly to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the centre of the diagram is a yellow box with the word "Pauk HQ Bosnia." Can you please describe what the lines connecting that box to other parts of the diagram indicate.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the yellow box you could also see is directly connected to the 21st Corps, also to the Arkan's forces, which represented by Colonel Pejovic and Captain Sarac, and again directly to Colonel Bozovic, Colonel Ulemek, Stamatovic Frenki and Jovica Stanisic along the line there. At the head of the HQ in Pauk is Major General Mile Novakovic, Fikret Abdic's forces, 21st Corps under Novakovic. So actually, when you look at it, it's all well connected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that particular exhibit. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, during the time that you spent in the 21st Corps, did you become aware of a policy regarding the Croat population in the area of responsibility in the Kordun area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when I came to the area of the 21st Corps, which, as I said before, was the December 1991, most of the Croats were no longer in the area. There were some isolated pockets and small villages that still had some inhabitants, mostly elderly and sick. Talking to the other members of the corps and from my first-hand knowledge of the things there, the policy was to get as many Croats as possible out of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a difference of opinion between certain elements, Serb elements there, regarding how this should best be accomplished?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In my meetings with Colonel Ajdinovic and Colonel Zimonja, for example, when we discussed this as being a problem, there were two different approaches to the problem. One was a more violent one, which was suggested by Colonel Ajdinovic, and that was just, you know, eliminate them, kill them all and be done with it. Colonel Zimonja was for a more diplomatic approach: Have them leave the area under protection of JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both of these men, with this difference of opinion, were both members of Yugoslav army KOS division?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Two different strains, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Ajdinovic advocated this killing of Croats, was he referring to Croat soldiers or was he referring to the Croat civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Saying "Croats" meant to me anything that is Croat, whether civilian or military. What you have to take into consideration, there were no military elements within the RSK or the Croatian army, there were only civilians remaining behind, so if he said Croats, he meant the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let him explain his reference to two different strains, the two colonels --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- of the JNA but of different strains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remind us about the two different elements of KOS and describe that again for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ajdinovic representing the internal security, dealing with internal security matters of the country; and Colonel Zimonja dealing with external elements, meaning emigres, people like that, outside of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of a typical task that would be assigned to the external branch and a typical task that would be assigned to the internal branch, to help us understand the distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the external part, which is also known as the intelligence part of the KOS, was dealing with the potential threat against Yugoslavia outside of Yugoslavia; whether it's in Canada, Australia, Great Britain, or whatever, in the world. Ajdinovic's side, or internal security, as the name implies itself, any danger to Yugoslavia within the border of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described at the beginning of your testimony certain work that you performed in Great Britain and in Australia. Would members of Ajdinovic's branch be assigned to those types of tasks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during these discussions regarding what to do about the Croat population, were there ever any representatives of the Serbian DB present, such as Toso Pajic or others who you've described earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was considered to be a general problem for the sector that we were in, so you had police members present there, also the members of the DB, namely, Mr. Toso Pajic and Djuro Skaljac would be attending those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you characterise for us their approach to this problem of the remaining Croat population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, both of them were people from the area, so they were deadly against using of force because, I don't know, maybe they anticipated in the future they would live with them again as neighbours or whatever the case might be, so they didn't want anything really, really bad to happen to these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did part of this policy also include the suggestion that some Croats be permitted to remain in the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Generally, there were three reasons why those people were still in the area. First, and the most important as far as the 21st Corps was concerned, was the public relation part of it, meaning if any of the foreign organisations like ECMM or International Red Cross wanted proof that the Croats were still living in the area, they not had all been exiled, not all been killed, I would take him, with the other members of the delegation, to those villages and show them the living people there. That would be one reason. The second reason, that was to deal with the internal security. If things were too calm, internal security had, of course, had a reason where and how to create the problem which would escalate into breakage of ceasefire agreement, for example. And the third one, last but not least, it was always a source of the civilians for exchange with the Croatian side for the Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you to tell us a bit more about the second reason. And you've testified that the presence of these people were essential in order to escalate into a breakage of a ceasefire agreement. Can you please describe in greater detail what you mean.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have personally attended 27 meetings with the Croatian military side in Turanj crossing area, which is a point between Karlovac and Vojnic, where we have signed a ceasefire agreement which most of them would be broken before the ink got dry on the document. If I were to put the ratio of those things, probably 4:1 Serbs versus Croats. So for every four broken, one would be a Croatian broken one. Having people along the Kupa River -- I know whether the Court is aware, the Kupa River is a natural border between the RSK and Croatia. It's a heavily mined area, virtually impossible to penetrate. So those villagers living there, as I said they would be used -- in one particular instance, an elderly couple was murdered, really, on the pretext that they were giving signals to the Croatian forces across the river by a small candlelight in the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you called upon to go to the scene where this elderly couple had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the complaint came through ECMM and I had to lead a number of ECMM members to the area and that was the first time I went there myself. We observed the position of the window, the vicinity of the possible observant from the other side, from the Croatian military side, and it was really impossible for anybody to see a candlelight in the window at a distance of two kilometres

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you came to learn who was responsible for the murder of this elderly couple?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A gentleman by the name -- and I use "gentleman" very freely in this context, Jovica Vojinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the unit led by the Colonel Ajdinovic, known as anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you come to learn that this man was responsible for the murder of this elderly couple?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We became kind of friends after a while. Mr. Vojinovic had a wife who was a Croatian national living in Karlovac and he always pleaded with me to try to get her exchanged so she can come and live with him in RSK, which eventually I succeeded in doing. So he always felt that he owes me a lot and he always presented him -- presented me to his friends as being somebody very important in that respect, that I can help them with their families. So they kind of liked me, they get close to me, and this is when I would hear all these different stories or things being admitted personally by some of the members of the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in case it's not clear from the record, what was the ethnicity of this elderly couple?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They were Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you what his -- did he tell you whether he was involved in the murder of this couple?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he claimed that he personally threw them into the well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to asking you about a number of events, I'm going to ask that a map be placed on the overhead projector. It is page 20 of the map book that the Chamber has. This particular copy I would tender into evidence, under the regime that was established by the Chamber last week, as 336.SL, the initials of the witness. This copy does have some markings that he has made on it that I believe will be of assistance to the Chamber as he testifies about certain events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not sure I'm with the suggestion of how we deal with this. It's in the map book, which we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of page 20 from the map book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What are you proposing? How are you proposing we exhibit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That it be given the number 336, which is the map book, ".SL" to indicate it's a copy of the map book that this witness has marked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the most convenient way of dealing with it. It may be more simpler to give these various additions to 336 numbers. I don't know if we've given -- I don't remember us dealing with this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We didn't deal with it regarding maps, but we did deal with this issue regarding I believe it was a photograph, and I had suggested to the Chamber that I would be asking different witnesses to mark up copies of the same photograph, and this was the regime that was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'd ask you to take a look at a copy of page 20 of 336, and I would ask you to first point out the original headquarters of the 21st Corps, Topusko.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, that tiny little dot there is Topusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the location of the office of the liaison officer of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the top of the hill just above the hotel in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to indicate for us where Vojnic is, the third and last headquarters for the 21st Corps.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have marked that in your handwriting on that photocopy of the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please show us where the Serbian MUP headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Located in Petrova Gora, which is here, and also they had their -- part of their HQ inside Bosnia, where the Pauk was, which is about here. It was like a split command between these two points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I will ask you later in your testimony about a parade held on St. Vidovdan Day, June 28th of 1995. Can you indicate on the map where that parade or celebration was held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the town of Slunj, just here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you marked that in your own handwriting on this copy of the map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about the Kupa River. Is that river visible on this map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it did not come through, but the line should go approximately like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the line --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This particular line, as I stated before, it was a kind of natural frontier between Croatia and the RSK, and our side of the Kupa River was heavily mined. And then you had a few of these little villages. Unfortunately, on this map they're not marked. But they're between Popovic Brdo, which is here, all the way down to Gornji Sjenicak, Sjenicak Lasinjski, and there's a number of small villages in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the locations that you have marked on Prosecution Exhibit 336.SL, which of these are in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the locations that you have marked, can you tell us which ones are actually in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All except Pauk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Pauk located?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the first event that I want to draw your attention to is in 1990, and it is regarding a log barricade. Did you ever have occasion to be present at a log barricade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Out of curiosity more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us approximately where this barricade was erected.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was in one of the roads leading to Knin area. It was back in 1990. I took a car and drove down with my wife. As I said, I wanted to see for myself what is it all about. I came to a number of felled trees positioned on a road that you actually had to drive like in a zigzag sort of thing, you can't go straight through, and there were a number of people standing at those barricades. They were not dressed in uniforms; however, they were armed, they had automatic weapon with them. Along both sides of the road there were a number of cars and trucks parked, which I had observed that some of them had Belgrade number plates on them, and also some of the trucks had JNA number plates on them. Me being a Serbian, I stopped there and I talked to the people and it was painfully clear that those people actually come from Belgrade by the accent and by the general lack of knowledge of the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the barricade that you witnessed, or you stopped at, was that part of what was purported to be a spontaneous event popularly known as "the log revolution"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what it appears to be. How spontaneous, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After -- let me ask this question first: Did you speak to some of the men manning the log barricades?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to them about where they were from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of the percentage of people at the barricade that you stopped at were local, from the area, and how many were from outside the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would safely place that percentage at around 75 to 80 per cent outside the area, meaning either from Belgrade or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after visiting this particular barricade, did you have a conversation with Colonel Zimonja about the log barricade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had, and he laughed the whole thing off, saying that the most of the people manning the barricades are actually from Belgrade, they were engaged over there. And according to Colonel Zimonja, they were paid 100 Deutschmarks a day for tending those barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time in 1990, were you -- or did you form a company that engaged the services of Serbian interpreters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have formed a company, was the only employee within it, so no other interpreters within the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Chamber the circumstances under which you formed this company.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a kind of long story, involved Mr. Abdic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from where did you receive the financial backing to form this company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Part of it came from the black funds of Colonel Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of this company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: YUIntra. It was kind of made from Yugoslavia Interpreting and Translating, YUIntra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps at this stage, would you just give us an idea of what was the purpose of setting up this company generally, and we can ask more specific questions later, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Zimonja believed I had a bona fide reason for staying in the region after losing the job with Agrokomerc. They needed me there. So the only thing -- I mean, Agrokomerc was the only employer in the area, so to stay there, there was a need to form something that would keep me there. So the company was the simplest solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the purpose of your remaining in the area to continue your work with KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention now to the early summer of 1991 and ask you whether during that time period Colonel Zimonja asked you to attend a meeting in Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you first begin by telling us who else attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A message came through a civilian person for me to go straight to Vojnic. Vojnic is only about 15 to 17 kilometres away from Velika Kladusa, where I was at the time. When I arrived there, the meeting was held at a local police station, in the office of Mr. Toso Pajic. The other persons which I remember distinctly were Djuro Skaljac, Colonel Ajdinovic, Colonel Zimonja, and probably another two or three police officers which I don't really remember their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police officers whose names you cannot remember, were they local police officers or from outside the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They were not local police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell whether they were from somewhere in the Krajina or from some other part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, they have never taken place in the discussion, they never talked, they were just there observing, I guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, in general terms, what was the topic of discussion at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was to describe the general situation in Velika Kladusa area, because the JNA contemplated an attack on a town called Cetingrad, which is just outside of the Bosnian border on the Croatian side, probably about two to three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was occurring in Cetingrad at this time? Was there armed conflict going on there at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time, no. But there was a very strong presence of Croatian emigres from Sweden organising the HDZ, the political, and some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paramilitary, according to the intelligence report given by Colonel Zimonja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were different proposals for an attack on Cetingrad discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two suggestions, and both of these suggestions were forwarded to General HQ in Belgrade to make a final decision. One proposed by Colonel Ajdinovic was to encircle the whole town, and then use the artillery, saturation bombing, and then just come in with a force and clean out the city. That was one. The other one, proposed by Colonel Zimonja, who was more interested in intelligence part of it, he wanted to leave a little corridor open between Cetingrad and Velika Kladusa for people to be able to leave the area prior or even during the artillery attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this discussion about Cetingrad, were there any actual incidents, that you are aware of, of paramilitary fighting coming out of the town of Cetingrad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, not prior to the JNA attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that the JNA -- or did the JNA attack Cetingrad, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Eventually, they did. It was in October. I was in Kladusa with other people from Kladusa, observing the actual -- you know, the lights in the sky from the artillery shelling, and immediately after the attack has started, the influx of refugees from the Croatian city of Cetingrad started arriving to the Bosnian city of Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it clear to you, by the nature of the attack, which one of the alternatives or proposals had been adopted for the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was rather obvious that the suggestion of General -- I'm sorry, Colonel Zimonja was accepted, because there was a corridor open for these people to leave through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based upon standard operating procedure and your experience of the 21st Corps, at what level would the decision have been taken regarding which proposal to implement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would have to be on the level of General HQ in Belgrade. We also have to remember, at the time it was still official JNA as a force on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to December of 1991 and ask you whether you were assigned to a specific task regarding two brothers by the name of Brajdic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have -- as I said, I attended a number of meetings in Vojnic in that particular period. Quite frequently, actually. On one of these meetings, since the influx of the Croatian in Velika Kladusa was worrying, it was suggested that some of these more prominent figures on the Muslim and the Croatian side should be eliminated, and possibly in one attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you ever assigned to eliminate any of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The task was given to me as knowing the area, being there, and two JNA officers. One was a rank of captain, another was the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you this assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ajdinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what specifically was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a little coffee-come-restaurant, if you like, in Kladusa called King, and it was to happen on Christmas Eve, on the 25th of December, when all these people would be there, celebrating prior to going to the midnight mass, I guess. And we were to approach from three sides, park the car in the vicinity, approach the restaurant from three sides and open fire from automatic weapon to everybody inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry out this assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Four or five days prior to the attack, these two officers came to Velika Kladusa fully dressed in JNA uniform, and as I was sitting in one of the coffee bars with a number of prominent Muslims from the local area, they came to me. They were drunk and they were carrying on about me being a great Serb and everybody should respect me for it, and all this will be part of Serbia, and generally they made it very uncomfortable for me. So I refused to deal with them any further after that. I didn't take them to be serious at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this particular time, you are still wearing the uniform and officially associated with the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I'm a civilian at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, upon the direction of Zimonja, that you joined the ARSK, the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That came on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time as a member of the ARSK, did you receive a salary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was more -- in ARSK, yes, I have received a salary. But there are some additional funds involved as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the different sources of funds that you received during your tenure with the 21st -- the ARSK army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was a general salary given to all the officers and the soldiers of the 21st Corps through the paymaster, and also I have received additional funds directly from Colonel Zimonja for which I have never signed for. In the first instance, yes, I would sign like any other regular officer drawing his salary and signing for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early 1992, did you have a conversation with Colonel Zimonja regarding the fact that the JNA would be pulling out of Croatia and moving troops from Croatia into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a generally known thing that it is going to happen prior to the arrival of the UN forces on the ground. The general conversation that we had at the time was how to organise people who are leaving behind, who are not leaving with the JNA. Personally, what am I supposed to do there, what is expected from me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he discuss with you what was expected of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, his task given to me was to go to the Samarica HQ, which was the HQ of the 8th Operational Group of JNA, led by General Mrksic, and to report to him as his liaison officer for the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many times did you work as an interpreter for Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would put between February, March, April, probably 20 or 30 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, continuing in 1992, did there come a time when you were instructed by Colonel Zimonja to attempt to recruit UN and ECMM staff for intelligence purposes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That was part of a daily routine really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what your understanding of your assignment was.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, to establish a kind of relationship where it would be easy for me to obtain necessary information, military side of it, through the UN HQ. That would involve, for example, a radio room, personnel with usually after the rank of sergeant, military observers, sometimes not to report what they had seen already, different battalion commanders. Well, really, I mean, anybody who was available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the process that you would undertake to recruit somebody working for the UN or ECMM.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It would be necessary for me to spend a considerable time with that. It wouldn't happen in a day. I would have to get to know them for two or three weeks, get as close to them as I possibly can, being really friendly, doing all the favours they ask for, approving everything they need, providing escorts for them in the sense of security, so they really felt that I'm a part of the team, I'm really helping them out. And at the same time, trying to find the weakest points in each of the members, which can be used for either purpose of a blackmail at some later stage or to exploit at any given time. I have to tell the Court that some of these people actually readily accepted to work with the Serbian side, some from purely ideological points, they believed in the Serbian cause; some of them for the reason of money; some of them for different reasons. I'm not saying everybody was, you know, possible to buy, but some have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you also receive instruction from Colonel Zimonja to report and track the activities of ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was a daily task for me. If there were -- see, at the very beginning, the ECMM were not allowed to sleep over in RSK. They would be escorted in the evening across to and back to Croatia, back to Zagreb, and they would return the next morning. But eventually the green light was for them to stay within the area and I would move in a hotel where they were and I would be there virtually 24 hours with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of you monitoring ECMM personnel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, control the movements of the ECMM, meaning more or less they would like to have full independence of movement, which they never really had, because they either would have a military escort or a police escort with them if they're going into the field. I would be there in the sense of monitoring who they talked to, who they stopped, where they stopped, who made telephone calls on their mobile phone in the vehicle they had. So generally, it was just to monitor whatever they do and report, daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you characterise your work during this period as facilitation or obstruction of their mission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As a sword with two very distinct differences. I was to facilitate as far as allowing them to move freely so I can find out who they get in touch with, and yet make it as difficult as possible for them to see everything they want to see. So there is a part of obstruction and part of facilitating. So it kind of worked hand-in-hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a specific example of how you would obstruct the work of an ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that in the evening they would inform me they need to go to certain specific area the following morning. That is their routine. And during the night, if we didn't want them to go there, we would create a little incident in the vicinity of the place and when they would turn in the following morning and say Can we go there? We would say, No, we can't go there because there is this major ceasefire being broken during the night there and that is out of limit area right now. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the incident that you -- that would be created, who would create it, who would execute it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was one unit who was responsible for all disturbances there, and that was the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during this period that you had a conversation with Colonel Bulat regarding this obstruction of the work of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was very clearly and very specific that they should not be allowed to carry their task, whatever their task was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you at whose direction this task of obstruction came from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the obstruction was actually more demanded by Toso Pajic than it was by Colonel Bulat. He was more concerned by the state security than the military itself. All our units were deployed well away from the road, so ECMM driving along the road couldn't see much to report to the Croatian side, yet from a security point of view, the DB was more concerned about who they talked to and who they're dealing with. So it was actually the both sides -- I mean, the DB and the military were concerned about freedom of movement, which is guaranteed to the ECMM and yet it was obstructed by us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Toso Pajic indicate at whose direction he was implementing this obstruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask now that Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 6, be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, I'd ask you to look at this picture and tell us: Do you recognise the people depicted in it? Can you please describe if you recognise the people who are in the picture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the gentleman with the profile over here, I really can't remember who he was, and I can't see it on the photograph. The gentleman next to him is Colonel Tarbuk, Slobodan, he was the commanding officer of the 39th Corps. The gentleman next to him in the blue beret is Brigadier General Musa Bamayi of Nigeria, who served as a sector commander of the UN. Next to him is chief of staff of the 21st Corps, Colonel Cedo Radovanovic. Then we have Toso Pajic. On his shoulder, you can see the police patch there. And then me as liaison officer. That was one of the meetings within the UN building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in 1992, were you given the task of recruiting interpreters that would be used by international organisations working in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was obvious at the time once the UN moved into the area there will be a number of job openings for the local populace, from interpreters down to the dishwasher or cleaners, whatever the case might be. And it was of interest to us to monitor those working for the UN for the benefit of gathering intelligence through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from whom did you receive this instruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again it was a joint operation of the state security and intelligence part of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us the names of the people who specifically communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nikola Zimonja and Mr. Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe how you carried out this assignment.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In official form, a letter was forwarded to the UN HQ in Topusko, saying that if they advertise for the positions there and they have people showing interest for them, they have to be cleared by police to prevent the criminal element of being employed within the UN. So they would like to have our own background check of the people. What we really wanted to know is who is expected to work there so we can get in touch with them first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the United Nations comply with this request to provide the names?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Unwillingly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you were provided with the names of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would have a little briefing with them, addressing their inner patriotic thoughts about what they are actually doing, they are doing it for the benefit of their own country, gathering information about military movements, about Croat movements. Because it was no secret that the military observers which would be travelling along the border or the DMZ, the demilitarised zone between Croatia and RSK, would observe also the movements of the troops on the other side. Coming back to the UN HQ in Topusko, they would write their reports and if any of our people could get their hands on that report, great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some of these people take UN reports and provide them to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one of these interpreters that you approached refused to cooperate in the manner you've described, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He would be discredited and not be permitted to work for the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what percentage of these interpreters do you have first-hand knowledge and first-hand experience with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Within the area of the 21st Corps?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 35 to 40, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that all of the interpreters or were there other interpreters that you did not have contact with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Within the 21st area Corps, there were no other interpreters. They had to go through me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of those 35 to 40 interpreters, how many were working for you gathering intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you do with the intelligence information and documents, if provided, that you received from these interpreters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me first try to describe very briefly what interpreter's job was there. They would attend the meetings between the local politician, for example, local Red Cross, the UN, and I would have all these other interpreters attending those meetings because I couldn't personally be there. I can't be physically in all those places. So I would have them go and come back and report to me about what was discussed at the meeting, what decisions were made, if any was made, and then I would compile all these reports in one major report which was sent to my HQ. I would do those in triplicate, really, because one was going to Colonel Zimonja, one was going to the HQ Colonel Bulat, and one was going to Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a copy of your report was going to KOS in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the copies went to Toso Pajic, who you've testified was working for the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last one went to Colonel Bulat, who was in charge of the 21st Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And it was his area of operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now move to 1993. Did you have occasion to attend a number of international conferences designed to try to come to some agreement regarding peace in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have personally attended four of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to -- or during your attendance at these international conferences, were you still an active member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and active member of the RSK army. I mean, I was part of the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to leaving for these conferences --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have water or ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to leaving for these conferences, were you issued any false identification documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been issued with three passports. All three would indicate that I was not -- two would indicate I was not born in Belgrade but born in Knin, and one would be an original one with place of birth and date of birth and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, before it is placed on the overhead projector, I'd ask you to leaf through the several pages of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to speak about them as I go through?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to select the page where it indicates where you were born, and that is the page that I would ask be placed on the overhead projector. And I would ask you to indicate for us, using the pointer, where it indicates your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 26th of February, 1947, Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that false information regarding your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This passport was issued to me on the 21st of June, 1993. You can see that on the bottom of the page, where I'm pointing now. The purpose of this passport was to attend international meetings and prevent anybody asking why is a person from Belgrade attending a meeting that deals with the Krajina? So this shows a passport that says you were born in Knin so you have full right to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you this passport?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Both of these passports, this one and the other one -- this one here, for example, which is -- if I can show that. This one here is passport of service. I had two passports. One was a diplomatic passport and the other one was a civilian passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that document is also Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And both of these passports, actually three passports, were issued to me in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who actually gave you, physically handed you the passport?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Secretary of then President Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd now ask that Prosecution Exhibit 348, tab 8, be placed upon the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Some of them, yes. Actually, I recognise all of them, but I remember only the names of some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the handwriting that is on this photograph, is that your own?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to go from left to right and indicate who the people are depicted in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The first chubby, bald guy, that's me. Next is Admiral Dusan Rakic. He was then Minister of Defence of the RSK. The gentleman at the back, I know he was to do something with security of President Hadzic, same as this guy here. And that's President Hadzic, and that's his secretary, private secretary. She is the one who gave us the passport and the money while we were there. Anyway, this photograph is taken in Norway during one of those supposedly secret meetings between the Serbian, Croatian, and the UN. And this large gentleman here, I also can't remember who he was really. I don't think it's somebody important. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, prior to talking about specific conferences that you attended, I want to ask you to describe in general terms the procedures involved prior to attending one of these conferences. And can you describe for the Chamber how it -- you would come to learn that you were going to be going on one of these conferences?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me begin with the request for a conference would usually come through the UN. The Croatian side would place a request to the UN Zagreb HQ, which in turn would inform the sector HQ of the UN in the sector which I was in if the meeting had to do something with the area of the 21st Corps. That would go the same for the 39th. On a general level, if it was to do with -- on the level of the government, then the Knin would be informed about the request by the Croatian side that they are willing to have a meeting. We would then proceed in arranging the delegation, the military and the civilian. We would request an agenda to be given to us in advance about what are we going to discuss during this meeting, usually under the pretext we need to get prepared for those meetings by knowing what's on the schedule of discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would this request be made to? This request for an agenda, who would this request be directed to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would the UN comply with this request and provide a proposed agenda?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing strange in asking for an agenda in advance really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue with your description.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Once all these little details were sorted out, it was expected from us, as a delegation, to be at least 48 hours prior to departure to wherever we're going, to be in Belgrade. We would usually be placed in Hotel Mladost, which is in the central part of Belgrade, in any case, which was always considered to be a home away from home for anybody coming from RSK, because I had never seen anybody paying any bills in this hotel if he had an RSK ID with him. They would have a series of meetings there. The head of delegation would go to Mr. Milosevic's cabinet for the instructions. The head of military would go to a military, to the HQ, for the instructions, because already, as I said, we had the agenda in advance. So these people would go, they would be advised how to and what to do during the meeting. They would come back, refer to us, tell us what is requested from the rest of the delegation. Myself personally would have a meeting with Colonel Zimonja, which he would give me a specific assignment during the meeting, whether it happened in Austria or Switzerland or Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these members of the delegation received their individual briefings, would there be a joint meeting held in the Hotel Mladost?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the conference room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who would attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All the members of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would be discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Whatever they were briefed, whether in cabinet of Mr. Milosevic or the General HQ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were these informal meetings or were they chaired by someone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: They were usually chaired by whoever was head of the delegation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if minutes were taken of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was done -- do you know what happened -- or first let me ask you: What kind of minutes were taken? Was somebody writing down verbatim what was said or was somebody simply writing down notes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a short reminder what we discussed, what we agreed upon, which we eventually sent to Knin, what the general consensus of the delegation is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would these minutes be sent anywhere else that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the course of the delegations that you attended, and can you tell us how many altogether you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I attended four; two in Geneva, one in Austria, and one in Norway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a general pattern of instruction to the delegates emerge over the course of these four peace conferences that you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very much so. They all look alike. The idea was not to agree on anything. That was very simple to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this meeting in Hotel Mladost, how would the delegate -- members of the delegation travel to wherever it was they were travelling? Would they travel together or separately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. We would travel together by the UN flight; the UN would provide a plane for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the different locations of where the conference was held, would the delegation remain together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of these conferences, were members of the delegation required to keep regular contact with Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only if they encountered a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us in general terms how this contact was maintained?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any of these meetings, whether it was held in Vienna or in Switzerland, we would have a separate room for adjournment during the meetings. At any given time during the meeting, we could ask for a recess. Let's say that the Croatian side had put a proposal about something and we're not prepared to give an answer immediately. We would say okay we've got to draw back, into our own little office over there, we will discuss amongst ourselves for a while, we'll come back to you and give you an answer. At the time which we were using in the office would be to get in touch with Belgrade, we were assured that the lines, telephone lines in the office were secure line, meaning nobody can overhear our conversation. And then the contact would be established with Belgrade, saying, well, this is what we have encountered, this is the request, what are we going to do about it? In some instances, the answer was just refuse. Simple as that. But if we're cornered, we run out of excuses, what do we do then? Well, then sign but make a stipulation that it has to be confirmed or approved by the General Assembly once you get back to RSK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these breaks in the conference when phone calls would be made to Belgrade, would you be present in the room?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would be in the same room where all of us are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to hear at least the -- your side of the telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I mean, they're not big rooms. They might be, I don't know, two metres by three metres. And you would have, like, ten, fifteen people sitting around the table.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over the course of the four conferences, were there some people in Belgrade that were regularly contacted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the level of Mr. Milosevic's cabinet, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please go through the name of each person who was regularly contacted and tell us who it would be that would contact that particular person.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At the meetings which were attended by the then President Hadzic, my understanding, he was speaking to Mr. Lilic at times, to some other unknown people from the cabinet of Mr. Milosevic that I really don't know. Anything to deal with the state security would be directed to Jovica Stanisic. Anything to do with the military part would be directed to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It all really depends upon the situation. I'm not talking that every meeting involved all these people to be phoned but if the event was purely military, then during our break we would call General Perisic and discuss the problem if there is a problem, or Stanisic or whoever. But mostly it was a political problem, so it was discussion with the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what types of problems for which Mr. Stanisic would be contacted and discussion had?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, at one stage it was suggested by the Croatian side that we should have a model village which would have Serbs and Croats put together in this village under the auspices of the UN and to prove to the world that they can live together as they did before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that Mr. Lilic was one of the people that was contacted. Is this the then-president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Zoran Lilic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he was referred as a postman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who referred to Mr. Lilic as a postman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Toso Pajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why Mr. Lilic was referred to as a postman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Carrying the messages from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they or you believe that he was making any decisions himself regarding the situation at the peace conference?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that Mr. Lilic made any decision in his entire life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if an agreement was to be communicated to the United Nations or to the other side, was there a caveat to making an agreement or binding the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was always very clear before even the meeting started that no decision will be made by the end of the meeting. Even if there is one, we shouldn't go away with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain for us the rationale, if you know, underneath this policy of not committing or making any agreement at these peace conferences?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Even officers are just people, so we would sit after the meeting, or even during the meeting or during the break and talk about it ourselves, and it was very obvious to us that Belgrade has no intention of settling the matter between the RSK and Croatia. As long as there is a problem over there, it will take the public view away from what is happening to Yugoslavia at the same time, meaning the great political unrest, the economic problems and so on. So as long as you have this brethren fighting for their bare survival in Croatia, the public eye would be on the RSK. So the idea was as long as we have a problem over there, people will look over there. So we don't want resolution of the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any policy regarding an attempt to appear cooperative despite this reluctance to commit to anything?
